explain.say: Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: the digestive system. Look at the oesophagus, the liver and the gall bladder. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

explain.say: Start at the mouth. Your teeth chew food into small pieces and saliva starts digesting starch. Then the oesophagus, a muscly tube, squeezes it down to the stomach. Now look at the stomach: acid and churning turn food into a soupy mix. Why might acid help?

faq.a: The stomach churns food with its muscle walls and mixes it with hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin, which starts digesting protein. The acid also kills many germs.

faq.q: What does the liver do in digestion?
faq.a: The liver makes bile, which is stored in the gall bladder. Bile breaks fat into tiny droplets, so enzymes can digest it faster, and neutralises stomach acid.
The pancreas makes digestive enzymes, amylase, protease and lipase, and releases them into the small intestine. It also makes the hormone insulin.

faq.q: What does the small intestine do?
faq.a: It finishes digesting food and absorbs the small molecules, like glucose and amino acids, into the blood. Tiny finger-like villi give it a huge surface area.
asks: Tell me about the small intestine

faq.q: What does the large intestine do?
faq.a: It absorbs water from the leftover undigested food, and its helpful bacteria make some vitamins. The remaining waste, faeces, is stored and then passed out.
asks: Tell me about the large intestine

facts: The human small intestine is about 6 to 7 metres long.
The internal surface area of the small intestine is roughly 30 to 40 square metres, about half a badminton court.
